title: How to Be a Faithful Citizen
excerpt: Scripture makes you a resident alien, a citizen of heaven who loves the country he does not worship. That is not a contradiction. It is the only way to be a citizen without becoming an idolater.
body:
The Bible gives the Christian a strange dual citizenship that the tribes keep collapsing into one. Paul says our citizenship is in heaven. Peter calls us sojourners and exiles, resident aliens whose deepest loyalty lies elsewhere. And the same Paul submits to the governing authorities, uses his Roman citizenship to demand justice, and tells us to pray for kings. The same prophets who relativize every nation command God's exiles in Babylon to seek the welfare of the city, to build houses and plant gardens and pray for the peace of a pagan empire.

So the faithful citizen is neither an anarchist nor a hermit. He is a resident alien who loves the country he does not worship, works for its good, prays for its rulers, tells it the truth, and serves his neighbor through its common life, precisely because his hope is not riding on it. Hold both halves and you have the only stable ground there is. Drop either one, and you have either withdrawal or idolatry.

## Seek the welfare of the city

God's word to the exiles in Babylon is the charter of faithful citizenship: seek the welfare of the city where I have sent you, and pray for it, for in its welfare you will find your welfare. Notice it is a pagan city, the very empire that carried them off, and they are told to work for its good anyway. This kills the idea that faithful citizenship means waiting for a Christian nation before you participate. You build, plant, and seek peace in the actual country you are in, flawed as it is.

This means showing up. Voting thoughtfully. Knowing your neighbors. Serving on the school board or the food bank or the jury. Telling the truth in public. The faithful citizen is present and useful, not because the nation is ultimate, but because his neighbors are real and the laws and structures shape their lives.

## Honor the authorities without worshiping them

Peter says honor the emperor, and he wrote it about an emperor who would later have Christians killed. Honoring authority is not the same as approving of it, and it is certainly not worshiping it. The Christian pays his taxes, obeys the just laws, prays for leaders he despises, and refuses the contempt that the culture treats as a civic virtue. Daniel served pagan kings with integrity and without flattery. Joseph administered an empire that was not his and did it honestly. You can give a government real honor while denying it the ultimate allegiance it keeps asking for.

And there is a limit, marked clearly. When the authorities command what God forbids, the apostles answered, we must obey God rather than men. Honor is real but not infinite. Caesar gets the coin. He does not get your conscience.

## Refuse the partisan capture of citizenship

The American argument will try to convince you that faithful citizenship means total enlistment in a party, that any Christian who will not fully enlist is naive or compromised. Both tribes make the same demand in opposite colors: give us your ultimate allegiance, let your hope and your fear be set by us. The ancient Christian ethic refuses this. A citizen of heaven cannot be wholly owned by any earthly faction, because his deepest belonging was purchased from every tribe and tongue.

This frees you to vote without idolatry and to disagree without despair. You can support a cause with conviction and still see its blind spots, because the party is not your god and its platform is not your scripture. The faithful citizen is the freest voter in the room, owned by no faction, terrified of no result.

## Tell the truth in public

The prophets engaged the public square mainly by telling it the truth, and they told it to kings who could kill them. Faithful citizenship includes a witness: naming injustice, defending the vulnerable, refusing the comfortable lie even when it serves your side. This is not the same as winning. It is bearing honest testimony in a country that increasingly rewards the lie that flatters the tribe. I have stayed silent when truth was costly and called it prudence. It was not prudence. It was fear, and the faithful citizen has to repent of it.

## This week

Do one concrete thing for the welfare of your actual city, with no partisan angle attached: serve a need, show up to a local meeting, help a neighbor through the common life of the place. Then pray, by name, for a leader you did not vote for, asking God to give them wisdom. You are a resident alien. Love the country. Do not worship it. The distinction is the whole of faithful citizenship.
